Uproar
ŭp´rōr
n. (a tumult, a riot; rendering Greek thorubos, stasis, and sugcheo, Hebrew hamah)
Dutch oproer, a stirring up; the English spelling was reshaped by roar. In Acts the word follows Paul from city to city.

Biblical Definition

The chief priests would not take the Lord on the feast day, “lest there be an uproar among the people” (Mat 26:5; Mar 14:2). At Thessalonica the unbelieving Jews “set all the city on an uproar” (Act 17:5). At Ephesus the town clerk warned, “we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar” (Act 19:40), and “after the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples” (Act 20:1). At Jerusalem “all the city was moved… and all Jerusalem was in an uproar” (Act 21:31), and the chief captain took Paul for the Egyptian who “madest an uproar” (Act 21:38). Adonijah's guests heard “the noise of the city being in an uproar” at Solomon's anointing (1Ki 1:41).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines uproar as great tumult; violent disturbance and noise; bustle and clamor.

UPROAR, n. Great tumult; violent disturbance and noise; bustle and clamor.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:5 — "But they said, Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people."

Act 17:5 — "But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people."

Act 19:40 — "For we are in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar, there being no cause whereby we may give an account of this concourse."

Act 20:1 — "And after the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples, and embraced them, and departed for to go into Macedonia."

Act 21:31 — "And as they went about to kill him, tidings came unto the chief captain of the band, that all Jerusalem was in an uproar."

1Ki 1:41 — "And Adonijah and all the guests that were with him heard it as they had made an end of eating. And when Joab heard the sound of the trumpet, he said, Wherefore is this noise of the city being in an uproar?"

Modern Corruption

The fear of an uproar governs what the church will say, which was the chief priests' policy and not the apostles'.

expand to see more

Matthew 26:5 records a leadership managing public order: not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar. They feared the people more than God, and their timetable was overturned by a traitor who made the feast day possible. The apostles went the other way. Paul's preaching produced an uproar in Thessalonica, an uproar in Ephesus, and an uproar in Jerusalem, and the complaint against him in Acts 17:6 was the finest description of the gospel its enemies ever gave: “These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also.” A ministry that has never caused an uproar has either preached to no one or preached nothing, and Acts 20:1 shows the apostolic response to a riot: when it ceased, he called the disciples, embraced them, and went on to the next city.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek thorubos (G2351), a noise, tumult; thorubeo (G2350), to set in an uproar; stasis (G4714), a riot, insurrection; sugcheo (G4797), to stir up, confound; Hebrew hamah (H1993), to roar, be in tumult.

expand to see more

Greek thorubos (G2351) — tumult, uproar; Matthew 26:5, Mark 14:2, Acts 20:1, 21:34; thorubeo (G2350), Acts 17:5.

Greek stasis (G4714) — riot; Acts 19:40; sugcheo (G4797), Acts 21:31; anastatoo (G387), Acts 21:38.

Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to roar, be in an uproar; 1 Kings 1:41.

Usage

"“Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar” — the priests' fear of the people."

"“Set all the city on an uproar” — Thessalonica's reception of the gospel."

"“After the uproar was ceased, Paul called unto him the disciples” — and went on."
